analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to rebook, feed, and lodge stranded passengers and prepare computer-outage recovery plans.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require airlines, when a delay over three hours, a cancellation, or a missed connection is the airline's own fault, to find passengers a seat on another carrier to their destination, and to accept displaced passengers from other airlines for a reasonable fee. It would also require airlines to provide food, hotel rooms, and ground transport for long delays they cause, give meal vouchers after four-hour delays, let passengers switch flights free of charge if a lavatory is broken, and file confidential recovery plans with the FAA so that computer-network meltdowns (the kind that have grounded entire airlines) are treated as the airline's responsibility. The Transportation Department would write the rules, and a government study of airline computer systems would follow.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers. Today, when an airline cancels a flight because of its own computer failure or crew shortage, it owes passengers little beyond a refund or rebooking on the same carrier — often days later. This bill would obligate the airline to shop the passenger onto a competitor's flight, pay for hotels and meals on overnight delays it causes, hand out meal vouchers after four-hour delays, and provide food, water, and restroom access during long tarmac-style waits. Passengers stuck near a broken-lavatory aircraft could change flights without a change fee.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Airline passengers on delayed or cancelled flights

how_it_helps.text: Airlines would have to seek alternative transportation — including on another carrier — for passengers displaced by delays over three hours, cancellations, or missed connections caused by circumstances within the airline's control, and would have to accept those passengers from other airlines for a reasonable fee.

For overnight delays the airline caused, it would have to pay for lodging, transportation to and from the hotel, and meals — or the cash equivalent if a passenger prefers — with an exception only for passengers living within 60 miles of the airport.
Airlines would have to provide meal vouchers (or cash at the passenger's request) for delays over four hours, and ensure food, water, restroom facilities, and medical assistance during long delays.
Passengers could switch off a flight without paying a fee if the lavatory is not working before departure.

Schedule changes from computer-network disruptions, security breaches, or other system failures could count as events within the airline's control — closing a gap airlines have used to escape responsibility for IT outages — and each carrier would have to file an FAA recovery plan for its critical computer systems.

analysis.who_pays: The major airlines, which would bear the cost of buying seats on other carriers for their stranded passengers, honoring meals and hotel rooms on delays they cause, and maintaining and documenting backup computer systems. Those costs would be passed partly into fares, but they are small relative to ticket prices and fall only on delays and cancellations the airline itself causes — bad weather remains excluded.

drawbacks.text: The bill carves out significant exceptions: lodging and meal obligations apply only to delays the airline controls, so weather cancellations — the most common cause — trigger nothing, and passengers who live within 60 miles of the airport get no hotel coverage at all.

The airline recovery plans filed with the FAA would be exempt from public disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act; only a general outline would be public, limiting outside scrutiny of how prepared each carrier actually is.

Requiring airlines to buy seats for displaced passengers on other carriers would add costs airlines would partly recover through fares, and leaving the Secretary of Transportation to define what counts as 'within the carrier's control' invites case-by-case disputes between passengers and airlines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are real but deliberately modest: they bite only when the airline itself causes the problem, and the compliance costs — rebooking fees, vouchers, contingency planning — are small against the scale of disruption passengers absorb today. The weakest parts are the 60-mile local-resident exemption and the secrecy around the filed recovery plans. On balance, a reasonable consumer-protection bill whose costs are far outweighed by the value of not being stranded overnight at your own expense.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Aviation Subcommittee on day one, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Daniel Lipinski introduced the bill on June 7, 2017, with Rep. Walter Jones joining as the original co-introducer.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day, and to the Subcommittee on Aviation the next day.
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The major airlines, which avoided mandatory rebooking on competitors, hotel and meal obligations, and computer-recovery plan requirements — all rules that later years of congressional and regulatory pressure on airline customer service never required of them during this period.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major airlines, which avoided the new obligations

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Rep. Bill Shuster, R-PA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; it stayed with the committee and its Aviation Subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: U.S. airline industry
against.role: Major air carriers and their trade association
against.what_they_did: The industry has consistently opposed government-mandated passenger compensation and rebooking requirements, which would impose costs no U.S. rule then required.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat introduced the bill with a Republican co-introducer, and no roll-call vote ever occurred, so the fight never took a partisan shape in the record.

industries.note: The bill would impose real but bounded costs: buying seats for stranded passengers on other carriers, providing meals and hotels on delays the airline causes, and documenting computer-backup plans. Airlines' interest in avoiding those obligations runs against passengers', since the alternative is passengers absorbing the cost of airline-caused disruptions themselves.

The bill mandates FAA-filed network recovery plans, backup systems, and an industry working group on computer resiliency — work airlines would need vendors and consultants to perform, and a GAO study of carrier network architecture.

A mandatory interlining requirement — airlines accepting each other's displaced passengers — would push more rebooking traffic through other carriers and intermediaries, modestly reshaping where that business flows.
